canberra.title: Rosalie Gascoigne – the definitive retrospective exhibition at the NGA
canberra.snippet: Although Rosalie Gascoigne was born in New Zealand, she moved to Canberra when she was 26 and stayed for the remaining 56 years of her li...
canberra.content:
31 October 2026

Join the conversation

3

Installation view, Rosalie Gascoigne, National Gallery of Australia, Kamberri/Canberra, 2026, © Rosalie Gascoigne/Copyright Agency. Photo: NGA.

Although Rosalie Gascoigne was born in New Zealand, she moved to Canberra when she was 26 and stayed for the remaining 56 years of her life. Keeping this in mind, we can claim Gascoigne as a Canberra artist and, more controversially, argue that she was the most nationally acclaimed visual artist that Canberra ever produced.

She was also one of the most unconventional, non-First Nations artists, in her career trajectory. She was not an art school product and was quick to point out that she lacked the basic skills of draughtsmanship or knowledge of painting techniques nor had acquired the traditional bag of tricks associated with sculpture. She was also 57 when she held her first exhibition, but then continued at a pace until her death at the age of 82.

Rosalie Gascoigne, Suddenly the Lake, 1995, National Gallery of Australia, Kamberri/Canberra, given by the artist in memory of Michael Lloyd 1996, © Rosalie Gascoigne/Copyright Agency. Photo: NGA.

From the moment she embarked on her art career with a solo exhibition at the Macquarie Galleries, Canberra, in June 1974 and a more significant exhibition at Gallery A in Sydney in April 1975, her rise in the art world was meteoric. There was a major survey of her art at the National Gallery of Victoria in 1978. In 1982, she represented (with Peter Booth) Australia at the Venice Biennale (the first Australian woman artist to do so) and was the subject of major exhibitions at the National Gallery of Art, Wellington in 1983 and National Gallery of Australia in 1996.

Gascoigne was born in the same year as Sidney Nolan, 1917, however by the time Nolan turned 20, he decided that he was to be an artist and by the time he turned 50 he was offered a retrospective exhibition at the Art Gallery of New South Wales and had paintings in the Tate in London and at the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

By the time Gascoigne was 50, she had been doing ikebana classes (the traditional Japanese art of flower arrangement) for about five years with Norman Sparnon, a Sydney-based and Tokyo-trained master who came to Canberra once a month and taught the modern, 20th-century style known as the Sogetsu school, founded by Sofu Teshigahara.


Rosalie Gascoigne, Metropolis, 1999, Art Gallery of New South Wales, Gadigal Nura/ Sydney, gift of the artist 1999, © Rosalie Gascoigne/Copyright Agency, image © Art Gallery of New South Wales. Photo: AGNSW.

She was married to the astronomer, Ben Gascoigne, and they initially lived at the Stromlo Observatory where they had their three children. In 1960, the family moved to Deakin and by 1969 to Pearce into a house designed to their needs.

We are now familiar with the biographies of First Nations artists, who start exhibiting publicly in their late 50s or 60s, but had actually been acquiring their skillsets gradually for decades before their public flowering. One can argue that Gascoigne for decades was acquiring skills in arranging found materials – abandoned farming machinery, road signs, battered sheets of old, corrugated iron, discarded kitchen enamelware, bird feathers and fencing wire, initially to use in her Ikebana flower vase arrangements and later in freestanding assemblage sculptures.

Rosalie Gascoigne, Cow pasture, 1992, National Gallery of Australia, Kamberri/Canberra, purchased 1993, © Rosalie Gascoigne/Copyright Agency. Photo: NGA.

The exhibition at the NGA exactingly brings together a magnificent cross-section of Gascoigne’s work from her early box-like installations, bone sculptures, the linoleum works, the lively parrot pieces to the iconic constructed landscapes from soft-drink boxes, bee boxes and reflective road signs. The exhibition includes her seas of floating rusted corrugated iron, the profoundly moving feather pieces and her late, sombre weathered formboard works made in 1999, the year of her death.

Gascoigne burst onto the art scene precisely at the moment when it was receptive to new approaches, unconventional materials and to installation art and environmental art. Her genius was to become a collaborator with the weathered elements in nature and to create an image of our environment that seems authentic and true to our experience.

Rosalie Gascoigne, Plenty, 1986, National Gallery of Australia, Kamberri/Canberra, purchased 1987, © Rosalie Gascoigne/Copyright Agency. Photo: NGA.

Throughout Australian art, there have been artists who have made us see our environment with fresh eyes, for example Fred Williams, where many of us will see a Fred Williams landscape on our travels throughout Australia. Gascoigne also rediscovered the Australian landscape and now it is difficult when we see Lake George or the sweeping plains of the Monaro, not to see them through her eyes.

Rosalie Gascoigne, Feathered fence, 1978-79, National Gallery of Australia, Kamberri/Canberra, gift of the artist 1994, © Rosalie Gascoigne/Copyright Agency. Photo: NGA.

Deborah Hart, the Head of Australian art at the NGA, is the curator of this magnificent and definitive Gascoigne exhibition and the accompanying scholarly monograph that places her art within an art historical context. The show celebrates the profound lyricism of Gascoigne’s art – an artist who has made us see our environment with fresh eyes.

Greg Weight, Rosalie Gascoigne, 1993, National Portrait Gallery of Australia, Gift of Patrick Corrigan AM 2004. Donated through the Australian Government’s Cultural Gifts Program, © Greg Weight / Copyright Agency, 2026. Photo: NGA.

Rosalie Gascoigne, National Gallery of Australia, level 1, Galleries 2-7, 24 October to 14 February, daily 10 am to 5 pm.

No admission charges.

canberra.title: ‘A shell of a human’: How one nang spiralled into drug-induced psychosis for Sam
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article discusses problematic drug use and addiction. Sam Bramman was 19-years-old, recently graduated from high sc...
canberra.content:
Sam Bramman has since founded No2Nangs, advocating for law reform around access to nitrous oxide. Photo: Supplied/Sam Bramman.

CONTENT WARNING: This article discusses problematic drug use and addiction.

Sam Bramman was 19-years-old, recently graduated from high school and enjoying the freedom of being a young adult when he was offered a nang at a house party.

Nangs contain nitrous oxide (also known as laughing gas), which is an emerging drug of concern.

“I was under the assumption nitrous oxide was harmless, giving a short-lived high – a party drug,” Sam said.

“So I decided to try it.”

Upon receiving that first hit, Sam found he couldn’t stop thinking about the high.

Within a matter of weeks he became fully dependent on nangs, inhaling them in secret and while he was driving.

“I was trapped by the cloud of addiction, I thought what I was doing was ok,” Sam said.

Short-term use of nangs can cause dizziness, frostbite, loss of coordination and impaired judgement.

Long-term use or heavy usage can lead to neurotoxicity (due to related vitamin B12 deficiency), psychosis, hypoxia and death.

Six months into his addiction, Sam was trapped in a drug-induced psychosis.

He became paranoid, rejected his family and friends as they questioned his behaviour and thought the police were after him.

“I took off to the Gold Coast in my car – sleep deprived and using nangs,” Sam said.

“Once there, there were moments where I was walking around the streets screaming, not making much sense, walking barefoot with bleeding feet, using a charging cable as a belt.

“I really was not well.”

Sam remained in touch with his family over the phone during this time and his parents flew to the Gold Coast to find him.

They took an agitated and aggressive Sam to Byron Bay Hospital, where he needed to be sedated before ending up as an involuntary patient in a psychiatric ward at Tweed Heads.

He spent two months in the hospital, getting sober and onto medication.

“In that time, I was still really unwell, but the cloud of addiction cleared up,” Sam said.

Upon his release, he spent the next 12 to 18 months as “a shell of a human”, barely able to get out of bed.

“[I had been] such a ‘normal’ high school graduate and then my life – in such a short period of time – turned absolutely horrible,” Sam said.

As he continued to recover, Sam went back to the gym. He was then inspired to run from Sydney to Canberra to raise awareness and fuel law reform to make it harder for people to access nitrous oxide.

Sam’s especially concerned about how easily anyone can order “huge, fire extinguisher-sized nangs” online with same-day delivery.

“I have the passion to try all that I can to make sure other people don’t go down that path,” he said.

When Sam arrived in Canberra, he also spoke with Health Minister Dr Marisa Paterson about his concerns.

The ACT Government recently committed to introducing law reform to reduce the sale of nitrous oxide to Canberra’s minors.

This was also a recommendation from the coroner following the nangs-related death of a teenager in 2023.

Sam ran from Sydney to Canberra earlier this year to raise awareness about nitrous oxide-use. Photo: Supplied/Sam Bramman.

The latest University of NSW Ecstasy and Related Drugs Reporting System (EDRS) report found use of larger bottles, cylinders and tanks to access nitrous oxide (61 per cent) had exceeded the use of traditional smaller bulbs (55 per cent) for the first time since monitoring began in 2023.

“This change raises concerns about the potential for higher levels of exposure and an increased risk of neurotoxicity among people who use the drug,” the report stated.

Both large and small containers were commonly purchased from corner and convenience stores (40 per cent), mainly between 10 pm and 5 am.

In 2026, about one in ten (13 per cent) of adult participants who reported recent nitrous oxide use also reported experiencing persistent neurological symptoms.

“Understanding whether the shift towards larger cylinders has contributed to increased levels of harm is therefore an important public health priority,” the report stated.

Only four per cent of participants reported difficulty accessing nitrous oxide.

The ACT’s laws are expected to target minors.

Now 22 years old, Sam would prefer nang usage to be restricted for all age groups.

But he said making it difficult for children to access nitrous oxide was a good place to start.

“It’s important that no-one falls into the trap of it, but especially the younger generation as it’s really bad for brain development,” Sam said.

“Restricting supply is one of the most practical ways to reduce the serious neurological damage, vitamin B12 deficiency and impaired-driving risks we are seeing.”

As for young people considering using nitrous oxide, Sam urged them to at least do the research before putting a new substance into their bodies.

“Don’t just listen to posts on social media and what your friends say,” he said.

“There’s plenty of research out there on every drug, look at what you’re actually using.

“Looking back, I’m so forever thankful that my parents were there for me …. even when I was pushing them away.

“If it wasn’t for them, I wouldn’t be here.”

If this article has raised concerns for you about drug usage, help is available. The National and Other Drugs Hotline is available on 1800 250 185 for confidential support, including information, referral and telephone counselling for people struggling with addiction.

If you suspect someone is experiencing an overdose, call Triple Zero (000).

canberra.title: Beers + brisket = a summer collaboration worth celebrating
canberra.snippet: Summer beers just got even better because cult-favourite Big Box Barbecue is setting up at the Capital Brewing Taproom. What’s better tha...
canberra.content:
31 October 2026

Start the conversation

Michael Box of Big Box Barbecue and Capital Brewing’s head brewer Wade Hurley toast to a delicious summer. Photo: Supplied.

Summer beers just got even better because cult-favourite Big Box Barbecue is setting up at the Capital Brewing Taproom. What’s better than beers in the sunshine? Beers in the sunshine with a whole load of smoked meat. Bring it on!

Big Box Barbecue launched in 2024, as owner Michael Box juggled his newfound love of low-and-slow, Texas-style barbecue with his work as a full-time chef. He left the kitchen stove for the smoker and, in 2025, graduated Big Box from market stalls to a brick-and-mortar store. Its launch saw queues down the block for their strictly limited menu.

Now, the business has expanded, and there’s more meat than ever before. And Capital Brewing Co is the new place to get it.

“Great barbecue and great beer have always belonged together. Our barbecue is big on flavour. You’ve got the richness of the Wagyu, the smoke from the ironbark, the salt, the pepper and all those beautiful rendered fats,” said Michael Box.

“A great crisp beer cuts through that richness, refreshes the palate and gets you ready for the next bite.”

It’s not the first time Capital Brewing Co has brought in an additional food truck to bolster its food offerings during the busy summer. And it makes sense: more variety for customers and shorter wait times across multiple food trucks, rather than a long wait for Brodburger.

Feast boxes like this will be on offer all summer, along with snacks and exclusive specials. Photo: Supplied.

The menu will include Big Box BBQ’s signature Black Opal Wagyu Brisket, dry-cured for 36 hours and then smoked for another 18 hours. This core offering will appear in barbecue boxes alongside other meats, perhaps twice-smoked lamb short ribs or sweet-and-tangy glazed pork ribs, plus a range of condiments and sides.

While the meat takes centre stage, the supporting roles are well considered at Big Box. When I first ordered their barbecue box, I was blown away by their Texas pit beans: baked beans catapulted to greatness with smoky brisket and rich molasses.

Whispers suggest prime rib steak is making an appearance, along with exclusive weekend specials throughout the summer as the smoker takes up residence in the Capital Brewing beer garden.

For Michael Box, a collaboration with Capital Brewing Co just made sense.

“We have had such a great relationship from day one with Capital that when we sat down together, we knew something great would happen,” he said.

“We both care deeply about the product, from sourcing the ingredients to the final interaction with customers. It’s about the experience.”

Big Box Barbecue will be available at Capital Brewing Co’s beer garden at 1 Dairy Road, Fyshwick, from 6 November and throughout the summer. They will be open Friday to Sunday from 11.30 am until sold out. Follow Big Box Barbecue on Instagram and Capital Brewing Co on Instagram.

canberra.title: How volunteers are dealing with a ‘very prickly and difficult’ problem plant along the Murrumbidgee River
canberra.snippet: A multi-year campaign is underway to purge wild blackberry from the ACT’s southern waterways, where the fast-spreading weed is suffocatin...
canberra.content:
About 900 new native plants are growing along the Murrumbidgee River to tackle an invasive species. Photo: Southern ACT Catchment Group.

A multi-year campaign is underway to purge wild blackberry from the ACT’s southern waterways, where the fast-spreading weed is suffocating local bushland.

With government funding, the Southern ACT Catchment Group is tackling dense infestations that wipe out biodiversity along riverbanks.

“You might naturally have 20 different small shrubs in an area, but you’re only going to have one when blackberry dominates,” executive officer Martine Franco said.

“It spreads through the river, and it’s very dominating, very prickly, and difficult to remove.”

Funding is coming through the Urban Rivers and Catchment Project, with the group partnering with Ginninderra Catchment Group and Molonglo Conservation Group as delivery agents.

In their branch of the program, Southern ACT Catchment Group focused on the Murrumbidgee River corridor and some nearby tributaries.

They’re working to replace blackberries with native raspberries and other native plants to limit erosion and diversify wildlife habitat.

“Blackberry can dominate … That means that a lot of species can’t move through it.

“You lose biodiversity, in the number of different species that live in any certain area.”

Since their project began, volunteers have planted about 900 native plants along the river to re-create more suitable habitats.

Ms Franco said the replacement plants were chosen because they create similar cover to the blackberry but don’t have the harmful impacts.

“Small birds really like the shrubs, and while blackberry can be a bit of a harbour for small birds, it’s also a harbour for rabbits and other pests,” Ms Franco said.

“Replacing it with a native shrub layer is good for lots of different biodiversity [goals], while also providing some habitat for the small birds.”

She said that once the blackberry is cleared, volunteers can step in and begin planting, an essential step to prevent erosion.

“You might have to treat it three times, but once you get rid of those [blackberry] canes, you’re then left with open ground.

“Open ground is a place where erosion can occur … Replacing it with a similar species that’s more native and not so dominating, like raspberry, means that you’re returning a native species to the landscape.”

Throughout the program, the volunteers have also used coir logs and strategic planting to stabilise the riverbank.

Teams have mapped weeds and flora across the area.

“That gives us a better idea of where we need to target our work,” she said.

“We’ve removed a lot of debris as well – 95 kilos’ worth … which is actually a hell of a lot of debris from the waterways.”

Ms Franco described the project as a chance for Canberrans to put “their energy and interest” towards protecting the “mighty Murrumbidgee”.

She also said their efforts, and similar projects, were key in helping the natural environment endure.

“I think the thing to understand about Australian vegetation is it is diverse, and it is messy. The messier and more diverse it is, the better habitat it is for native animals.

“There are all these things that a biodiverse environment can provide that blackberry alone won’t.”

The project is ongoing and is set to finish in mid-2027.

You can get involved by visiting the Southern ACT Catchment Group or Facebook.

canberra.title: Garran parents’ concerns about school route safety fall on deaf ears
canberra.snippet: Parents at Garran Primary School have identified unsafe crossings, missing footpaths and traffic hazards along children’s routes to...
canberra.content:
Safety concerns around Garran Primary School have prompted parents to call for safer crossings, improved footpaths and traffic-calming measures on surrounding streets. Photo: James Coleman.

Parents at Garran Primary School have identified unsafe crossings, missing footpaths and traffic hazards along children’s routes to school, but the ACT Government has confirmed it has no immediate plans to address their concerns.

Despite receiving a detailed community survey and meeting with a parent representative, the government has not committed to any new pedestrian crossings, traffic-calming measures or footpath improvements.

Instead, the requests have been added to an infrastructure priority list for future consideration, with no confirmed funding or delivery timeframe.

The Garran Primary School P&C Committee is seeking urgent attention to several roads surrounding the school, warning that children face risks well beyond the school gates.

“For children who walk, ride or scoot, the risks do not begin and end at the school entrance,” P&C president Robert Knight told Region.

“They arise along the surrounding streets, at road crossings and wherever footpaths are missing, inadequate or difficult to use.”

The committee has identified Gilmore Crescent, particularly between Kitchener Street and the Garran shops, as a priority for safer pedestrian crossings and traffic-calming measures.

It also wants improvements around Kitchener Street and Robson Street, along with missing or inadequate footpath connections on Robson Street and Harpur Street.

Parents have raised concerns about vehicles obstructing visibility, unsafe stopping near the school, wide roads near bus stops and footpaths difficult to navigate with prams or young children.

Their concerns are supported by a survey conducted in October and November 2025, which attracted 86 responses from parents, carers and community members.

Nearly seven in 10 respondents agreed or strongly agreed that fears of children being hit by vehicles discouraged them from allowing children to walk or cycle to school.

More than 90 per cent rated safer crossings and completing missing footpath connections as very or extremely important.

The survey also found approximately four times as many respondents said their children would always walk or ride if the identified safety improvements were made.

The P&C has welcomed the government’s installation of a temporary traffic island at the school driveway, restricting vehicles to a left-in, left-out arrangement, but says it addresses only one part of the problem.

“Our concern now is the safety of the wider journey to school,” Mr Knight said who is planning to discuss the concerns with the Minister in the next meeting.

An ACT Government spokesperson confirmed the government had received the survey and that a representative from its School Safety Program had met with a parent representative.

However, the response offered no commitment to specific works or a comprehensive safety review of the roads identified by parents.

“While there are no immediate works planned in the vicinity of the school in response to the survey results, the survey findings have been added to the School Safety Program’s infrastructure prioritisation list for future consideration subject to other priority works and the availability of funding,” the spokesperson said.

The government said it was monitoring pedestrian and motorist behaviour following changes to the school frontage as part of the school’s modernisation project.

It acknowledged that Garran Primary School, which has more than 800 students, is located in a busy precinct adjoining Canberra Hospital, generating significant traffic throughout the day.

However, it described the survey as representing a very small number of respondents calling it a “snapshot” of the traffic concerns.

Asked whether it would meet with the P&C and commit to a prioritised improvement plan, the spokesperson said the government would continue engaging with stakeholders and considering requests, subject to competing priorities and available funding.

No timeframe was provided for deciding whether any improvements would proceed.

The government’s response comes despite its stated commitments to improving road safety and encouraging children to walk and cycle to school. The ACT Road Safety Framework 2026–2031 sets a long-term goal of eliminating road deaths and serious injuries by 2050, while the Active Travel Plan 2024–2030 aims to make walking and cycling safer and more accessible.

But the P&C argues that encouraging active travel is of little value if families do not feel their children can make the journey safely.

“Promotion must be matched by infrastructure that makes active travel a realistic option,” Mr Knight said.

The P&C has requested a meeting with relevant ministers and government officials to develop a prioritised program of improvements, including funding and delivery timeframes.

“We recognise that not every intervention can be delivered immediately, and that engineering assessments and competing demands must be considered,” Mr Knight said.

australia.title: Storm warnings for Melbourne, Canberra, Sydney and Brisbane as cold front ‘packs a punch’
australia.snippet: BoM predicts hail, damaging winds and possible flash flooding across Victoria, NSW and parts of Queensland into Sunday Get our breaking n...
australia.content:
Storm warnings are in place for multiple capital cities across Australia’s east and south-east as a severe weather front sweeps across the country.

Heavy rain, winds and thunderstorms are forecast to hit Melbourne and eastern Victoria throughout Saturday afternoon as a cold front meets warm, humid air.

The storm front is then expected to travel further east, impacting Canberra and inland NSW before reaching the east coast on Sunday, stretching as far as southern Queensland.

The Bureau of Meteorology warned of possible flash flooding in some areas and potentially destructive winds of over 125km/h that could bring down large trees or damage property.

Melbourne and parts of Victoria recorded moderate rainfall and some lightning on Saturday morning, with a more intense band of thunderstorms forecast into the afternoon.

“It’s this follow-up band of storms which could pack a punch,” BoM meteorologist Angus Hines said on Saturday.

The storms are expected to impact Melbourne, parts of Gippsland, the north-eastern ranges, and north-central Victoria, with damaging winds the greatest risk.

The risk area will extend further north through inland NSW into the evening – up to Queensland’s southern interior and along the NSW coast south of Sydney around Wollongong and the Illawarra.

The forecast in these areas includes possible damaging winds, heavy rainfall and large hailstones.

“Expecting some very active storms here a little bit later on in the day, mid to late afternoon for many of these areas, and potentially not until the evening hours by the time we’re looking at storms getting out towards the east coast,” Hines said.

The focus of concern will shift further north on Sunday, with heavy rain and storms around Brisbane during the afternoon and early evening.

Severe thunderstorms were most likely for parts of the NSW mid-north coast, the northern rivers, parts of the tablelands and the Hunter region, with possible hail, heavy rainfall, flash flooding and destructive winds of more than 125km/h.

Areas that had recorded heightened rainfall in the past fortnight were also at risk of flash flooding, Hines said.

“If you do live through this area, tomorrow is definitely a day you’ll want to keep a watch on the radar to see if any big storms are headed your way,” he said.

A broader area of potential concern for Sunday stretches from Newcastle, north of Sydney, up to Gympie on the Sunshine Coast.

A severe wind warning is also in place across the mountains of northern Victoria and southern NSW, with wind gusts of more than 100km/h recorded on Saturday morning.

australia.title: Pocock faces off with pesticides boss over Australia’s use of weedkiller linked to Parkinson’s and banned in 70 countries
australia.snippet: Pesticides authority ruled in June that paraquat could be used with certain conditions, but experts warn the decision risks overlooking s...
australia.content:
While helping their dad tend watermelon, capsicum and tomato crops, Greg Smith and his two older brothers often ended up drenched in weed killer.

There were no worries in the 1960s about the widely used herbicide paraquat – no talk of exposure risks and no thought of wearing protective gear.

Over the ensuing decades, Smith’s father fell ill and died suddenly, his middle brother succumbed to motor neurone disease and the eldest is undergoing cancer treatment.

The 73-year-old cattle farmer has himself survived two types of cancer and was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease in 2022.

He believes the family’s fate was sealed by poisoning from paraquat and other farm chemicals while working on their property in Queensland.

“In the 60s, no one had boom sprays; they went along with a little old pump … and Dad would walk along behind, spraying the bushes each side,” Smith says.

“We were constantly in the spray.”

Smith is one of many scrutinising the federal government’s decision to allow the continued use of paraquat despite bans in more than 70 countries.

The highly toxic chemical, which destroys plant tissue upon contact, has long been associated with Parkinson’s disease.

Questions remain about the use of the chemical in Australia, with a Senate inquiry in the works and independent politicians and health campaigners continuing to sound the alarm about the risks.

The Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA) ruled in June that paraquat could be used with reduced application rates and closed-valve packaging to prevent physical contact.

There is a two-year grace period for products with previously approved warning labels and a phaseout on use across certain crops including sugar cane.

The authority ruled there was no convincing evidence of a “direct causal association between paraquat exposure from approved pesticidal uses and Parkinson’s disease”.

But the decision has baffled Australian and international neurological experts, who have criticised the authority’s review methods, particularly the omission of a landmark 2011 study.

That study and subsequent research found paraquat exposure is associated with 2.5 times the odds of developing Parkinson’s or 4.5 times for those who do not wear protective clothing.

Meanwhile, grain and sugar cane growers say the new restrictions limit their use of a chemical that reliably kills weeds, helps establish crops and supports no-till practices.

Paraquat also remains an important tool for cleaning up pastures, particularly as many weeds become herbicide-resistant.

The independent senator David Pocock has been a vocal critic of the ongoing use of paraquat in Australia, and established the Senate inquiry into the authority’s decision.

After his motion for the closed-door inquiry to hold public hearings was defeated, he instead grilled the authority’s executives at a budget estimates hearing on Tuesday night.

APVMA’s review included studies funded by major manufacturer Syngenta and considered research examining the effects of poisoning after only 30 days, Pocock said.

“Parkinson’s has a latency of years to decades,” he said.

APVMA’s chief executive, Scott Hansen, defended the review in a sometimes tense 30-minute exchange, saying the authority considered potential biases from both industry and health sector researchers.

“It’s weighted evidence of all of the studies that are produced,” he said.

Hansen said while paraquat was banned in 27 countries across the European Union, it was the result of perceived deficiencies in regulatory frameworks rather than health concerns.

However, the US neurologist Dr Michael S Okun’s review of the authority’s final report found it risks overlooking significant scientific evidence about Parkinson’s links.

Decades of research shows repeated associations between paraquat and the disease, Okun says, and important questions about chronic exposure remain unanswered.

“In medicine, we do not wait for every uncertainty to disappear before acting to prevent serious harm,” Okun, from the University of Florida Health, wrote to the inquiry.

“We weigh the evidence, acknowledge what remains unknown and make decisions that recognise the consequences of being wrong.

“Australia has an opportunity to apply that same seriousness to the neurological risks associated with paraquat.”

Grain growers Kirk and Lisa Jeitz, who run a 2,800-hectare farm near Esperance in Western Australia, say they go to great lengths to protect workers and the environment from harm.

That includes using tractor cabs with carbon filters, extensive weather monitoring to avoid spray drift and strict buffer zones around waterways, native vegetation and neighbouring properties.

The imposition of lower paraquat application rates will affect weed control, soil quality and carbon sequestration due to increased cultivation, they say.

“We ask the committee to recognise the controls farmers already use … and to make sure any changes are based on evidence, clearly explained and phased-in with practical help,” the farmers wrote.

A submission from Parkinson’s Australia says the burden of proof should lie with manufacturers to demonstrate paraquat is unlikely to cause harm.

“Until such evidence exists … Australia should immediately prohibit the use of paraquat to protect agricultural workers, regional communities and future generations,” the submission says.

Syngenta has long maintained there is no established link between paraquat and the disease.

APVMA’s restrictions informed the manufacturer’s decision to remove paraquat products from Australia, sparking uncertainty in the agriculture sector about long-term availability.

The company has previously criticised media reports focused on “emotional” stories of people with Parkinson’s.

Smith is tolerating Parkinson’s treatment well but is troubled with short-term memory problems and a tendency to trip over.

He can still ride a horse long after his neurologist told him he would have to give it up.

Sitting on his son’s farm, watching his baby grandson, Smith hopes for a fairer system.

“[Some farmers] want to be able to spray as much of this stuff as they want so they can kill weeds easier,” he says.

“What about the community, society or greater good for people overall?”

Inquiry submissions close on 18 November.

australia.title: Albanese looks for reset on world stage as ‘spot fires burn’ domestically and likely interest rate hike looms
australia.snippet: The prime minister will speak with King Charles and others at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda Get our...
australia.content:
As “summit season” begins, reaffirming ties with fellow leaders on the world stage could be a circuit breaker for Anthony Albanese amid domestic and economic woes, analysts have said.

But a likely interest rate hike, triggered by higher-than-expected inflation, while the prime minister is overseas will make his job – and the treasurer’s – even harder.

Albanese is attending the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda from Saturday.

He will hold talks with King Charles III and allies including the UK and Canadian prime ministers, Andy Burnham and Mark Carney, at the biennial meeting.

The discussions will constitute a well-needed reset after controversies over grant funding and pressures on inflation, according to Dr Zareh Ghazarian, an associate professor of politics at Monash University.

“It is a strategically important time for him,” Ghazarian said.

“He’s got a lot of spot fires burning domestically but this is going to be an opportunity for him to present himself to be much more on the front foot.

“There’s a lot of pressure, so this trip could just be a moment to reset the political debate for people … this is a critical moment to present himself as a world leader amongst other world leaders.”

Albanese will be away when the Reserve Bank hands down its next interest rate decision on Tuesday, with markets tipping a rise to 4.85%.

It would be the fifth interest rate hike in 2026 and a challenging situation for the government to navigate, amid continuing cost-of-living pressures.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Albanese emphasised the value of attending Chogm before his departure on Saturday morning. In a crowded international calendar, the Commonwealth is occasionally dismissed as irrelevant, an anachronistic relic of a former imperial era.

“The Commonwealth heads of government meeting is an important forum,” Albanese said.

“[It provides] an opportunity to work with some of our closest partners on shared challenges, including climate change, the preservation of our oceans, trade and investment and the rise of AI.”

The issue of historical slavery, and its ongoing legacy, is likely to be a key point of contention at Chogm.

Burnham, writing in the Guardian, said having “difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future” was the right thing to do.

“Not just because it is in our interests, but because the Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today.”

He called the transatlantic slave trade a “brutal and barbaric violation” of people “treated as property and worked to their deaths”.

“I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people, and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today,” he wrote.

Caribbean nations have made renewed calls for Britain to apologise for its role in selling enslaved people for profit, and for reparations, as the King toured the Caribbean.

Burnham said: “Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process and I am open to them.” But he said he did not believe reparations for slavery was the “right answer”.

Australia would not be a bystander to any debate about slavery and the slave trade.

Across the 19th and early 20th centuries, Australian agriculture relied heavily on “blackbirding”: the use of coercion, trickery, bribery and kidnapping to bring more than 60,000 Pacific Islanders to work as indentured labourers in Australia, primarily on Queensland’s sugar and cotton plantations.

The Chogm meeting will kick off a busy end to the year overseas for Albanese, with international summits in Turkey, the Philippines, China and the US in coming weeks.

The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, is currently in Atlanta, Georgia for the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting. The start of that conference has been overshadowed by the presence of Russia, with about one-third of the countries attending vowing to boycott the customary “family photo” if the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, was involved.

australia.title: Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson could make a final bid for freedom. What are the prospects of a high court appeal?
australia.snippet: After attempt at acquittal or retrial was dismissed, Patterson has 28 days to lodge an application for special leave to appeal to Austral...
australia.content:
After losing her bid for a retrial, the mushroom murderer Erin Patterson could take her fight to the highest court in Australia.

But her prospects of success are far from rosy, a legal expert says.

Patterson woke up at the Dame Phyllis Frost Centre on Saturday knowing she is unlikely to see beyond the four walls of the prison ever again.

Her appeal against her murder and attempted murder convictions failed on Friday as the Victorian court of appeal instead increased her sentence to life without parole, in line with a prosecution appeal.

Her offending was so shocking, the court said her 33-year non-parole period was inappropriate.

Removing a parole period was a rare move for an appeal court, the criminology and justice expert Brianna Chesser says.

“It really speaks to the gravity of the offending,” the RMIT associate professor says. “I was expecting the non-parole period to be raised, maybe to 37 years. But to remove it altogether was definitely a shock.”

Patterson will have 28 days to lodge an application for special leave to appeal to the high court of Australia. If she is granted special leave, she will then have a formal appeal hearing. But 90% of cases do not even cross that first special leave hurdle, Chesser says.

The Victorian court’s dismissal does not automatically give Patterson the right to challenge in the high court, Chesser says.

“The court only deals with cases that shape national law,” she says. “This case would be of particular importance because of the fact that it’s high profile. But you’d be looking for some sort of egregious procedural irregularity, some sort of human rights violation – something really serious.”

Chesser does not believe Patterson’s case falls into any of the categories the high court usually considers.

But she still expects the convicted killer to try.

“It would make sense that she’d run it to the very end and exhaust all possible avenues,” Chesser says.

Patterson deliberately served deadly beef wellingtons to her former in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, 70, and Gail’s sister Heather Wilkinson, 66, in July 2023.

The three guests died after the meal at Patterson’s Leongatha home, in regional Victoria, while Heather’s husband, Ian, fell seriously ill but survived.

She fought to quash her convictions, arguing she suffered a substantial miscarriage of justice and she should have a retrial.

“This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated and stands to be denounced in the strongest terms,” the court of appeal judges said on Friday.

Patterson is only the second woman in Australia to be sentenced to life behind bars without parole.

The first was NSW woman Katherine Knight, who was jailed in 2001 after stabbing her de facto husband to death, skinning him and then trying to serve his cooked flesh to his children.

australia.title: US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with Russia
australia.snippet: Marco Rubio pulls plug on traditional photo op at meeting of foreign ministers after about one-third of countries threaten boycott The tr...
australia.content:
The traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has been abruptly cancelled in the US after a host of nations – including Australia and the UK – refused to appear beside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pulled the plug after several European officials, the UK and Australia made it known they would boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such international gatherings.

Rubio still opened the talks in Atlanta with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.

“We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.”

About one-third of countries at the talks made it known they would not appear beside any Russian representatives.

European Union nations had made clear they would boycott any photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because … there is no normality with Russia,” Germany’s foreign affairs minister, Johann Wadephul, warned ahead of Friday’s session.

The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised similar. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said.

During the meeting’s opening session, Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as brutal and unjustified - in front of Lavrov - saying Russia’s illegal war had affected international markets and worsened global food security.

A spokesperson for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the group photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine.

“Our focus at the G20 remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy.”

The schism in Atlanta is yet further evidence of the rupture caused by the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its isolated president, Vladimir Putin, into the international community despite Putin’s ongoing war against Ukraine.

Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding – as is its opposition to Poland’s membership in the G20.

Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration’s not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will probably prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said.

That did not surprise the Polish deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, representing his country at its first time as a guest at a G20 meeting.

“We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters.

Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month’s G20 leaders’ summit hosted by the president, Donald Trump, in Florida a success.

Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous meetings, was not invited this year, with US officials saying it was a deliberate choice to include only formal members of the group. Poland, not a member, is seeking formal membership with US support.

But missing from the invitation list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top US officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.

“We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” Phindile Kunene, a spokesperson for the South African international relations minister, Ronald Lamola, said.

world.title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
world.snippet: There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective Cora Bailey has been encountering ill...
world.content:
Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.

In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).

Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site.

“We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.

Police told her that the scale of the illegal mining was too big for them to do anything about, she said at the time. About a week later, officers sheared away the grass that had partly hidden the zama zamas. But within a few days a smaller group had returned, although Bailey said they were now taking Claw’s water only for drinking.

South Africa’s police regularly trumpet their success in tackling illegal mining. On 19 October, they said they had arrested 71 suspected zama zamas across the country in the previous week.

However, researchers put the number of illegal miners in the tens of thousands. In 2019, Marcena Hunter, a researcher at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime, estimated that a tenth of South Africa’s gold production, worth about $1bn, was being exported illegally.

Police operations have also led to tragedy. In 2025, 93 bodies were pulled from a mine shaft in Stilfontein, after officers blocked food and water from being delivered underground.

Meanwhile, there is no end in sight to the dynamics driving illegal mining, including the high price of gold, poverty, unemployment, corrupt politicians and police profiting, and the failure of mining companies to fulfil their legal obligation to seal mining shafts when they cease operating.

South Africa’s modern history is tied to mining. In 1884, gold was found on a farm, sparking a gold rush that led to the creation of Johannesburg. Gold production peaked in the 1970s, but South Africa was the world’s largest producer, a title it held for more than a century, until 2007.

In 2009, Morris Viljoen, a geology professor at the University of the Witwatersrand, estimated that the reef that gave the university its name had produced more than a third of the gold ever mined globally. Claw is housed in the old offices of the Durban Deep mine, which shut at the turn of the century, having once lent its name to an Elton John song.

The city government claims there is still 40,000 tonnes of gold underground in the region. But, with the remainder lying ever deeper, the costs of recovering it have risen.

Mining companies are supposed to seal up old mine shafts and rehabilitate the environment around them. However, in 2025 there were “6,100 derelict and ownerless mines and 1,170 unsafe mine openings”, the mining minister, Gwede Mantashe, said in response to a parliamentary question.

Zama zamas have stepped into those voids left in the earth. While there is no comprehensive data on them, experts agree that a majority are from neighbouring countries, principally Lesotho, Mozambique and Zimbabwe.

The skyline south of Johannesburg is punctuated by the pale yellow ridges of mine dumps. Increasingly, the ground is also caving open.

For politicians seeking votes in local elections on 4 November, the culprit is clear: illegal miners. In May, Kenny Kunene, the Johannesburg council member responsible for transport, took journalists on a tour of sinkholes that he claimed were the fault of zama zamas, including a section of Wemmer Pan Road that had completely collapsed.

The road was once the main artery linking the city’s central business district to the south-eastern suburbs. In one section it has completely disappeared, now raw earth pitted with the holes where illegal miners have been digging.

However, when it comes to sinkholes, experts say zama zamas are being scapegoated.

Rosalind Morris, an anthropology professor at Columbia University, who has worked extensively with illegal miners, noted that the porous dolomitic rock to Johannesburg’s south and west becomes unstable when water is removed.

“The biggest culprit of sinkholes in South Africa is formal industrial mining, which dewaters at a scale of hundreds of millions of gallons of water removed from underground every day,” she said.

“There are areas where there is a lot of residual gold, which are being very intensely mined by zama zamas, and some of that definitely causes structural collapse, there’s no doubt about it. But the idea that this was invented or caused for the first time by zama zamas is completely fallacious.”

Zama zamas are also frequently blamed for violence in mining areas, including a September mass shooting in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg. However, David van Wyk, the lead researcher at Bench Marks Foundation, said culpability laid with the often-feuding gangs that controlled access to the shafts.

“The guys working in the mine are actually super-exploited cheap labour … The guys with the guns are the guys who take the gold,” he said. “They don’t go underground.”

In Khutsong, about 50 miles (80km) west of Johannesburg, illegal miners, local and foreign, kept the township afloat, said Vusi Cele, the youth secretary for the local branch of Mining Affected Communities United in Action, a campaign group that advocates for “artisanal miners” to be granted mining licences. “Without those rents, it’s a ghost town,” he said.

While Cele, 33, currently hustles above ground selling mobile phone covers and screen protectors, he said he too would mine if he could get a licence. “On the surface there’s peanuts,” he said. “Underground there’s money.”

world.title: Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job
world.snippet: Critics cite Lana Nusseibeh’s denial of accusations the UAE is fuelling Sudan war by supporting paramilitary RSF Members of the Sudanese ...
world.content:
Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term ⁠this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.

Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide”.

Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.

The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.

There was also strong criticism of Nusseibeh’s candidature at a virtual briefing by the Avaaz human rights advocacy group on Tuesday.

Ibrahim Alduma, who grew up in El Fasher and is the co-founder of the human rights organisation Sudan Action Hub, told the briefing that success for Nusseibeh would result in people losing faith in the UN.

“If this candidate [succeeds], how would we tell people on the ground that the United Nations is not an obstruction of the [rights of] the people of Sudan?” said Alduma. “How could the people – not only in Sudan, but other victims of wars and international criminals – trust that the UN will achieve some kind of justice?”

Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the ‌UN to hold powerful states accountable.”

Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”

On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch, said Nusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.

In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.

She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.

To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.

An ​informal security council poll earlier his month had ‌placed the former Costa Rican vice-president ​Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in ​the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.

At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”

He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”

Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.

“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”

Additional reporting by Kaamil Ahmed

world.title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr
world.snippet: Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website Lina Attalah,...
world.content:
Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.

Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.

According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups.

“Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.

Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.

Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions.

Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – follows the arrest of the entire six-person team at the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom.

The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing.

“This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.”

According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”.

Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict. Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”.

Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November.

Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen International issued a statement with several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves.

“Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.”

world.title: Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official
world.snippet: Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and pos...
world.content:
The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.

As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.

“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said.

“Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.

“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said.

Kaseya said leaders around the world should realise that although the brunt of the health crisis is affecting Africa at the moment, the situation could change. “We shouldn’t forget that at the beginning of Covid, many countries said there was zero risk of being affected, but a few months later, they became the hotspot,” he said. “We don’t want to see the UK and other countries become the hotspot.”

This outbreak, the 17th in the Democratic Republic of the Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history.

Ebola is a highly contagious, severe, and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies, such as during funeral preparations.

On 15 May, DR Congo’s health ministry declared an outbreak in Ituri province, though sequencing shows it had begun in February. It has now spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last week, in west Africa, Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus.

France is the only non-African country to have confirmed a case of Ebola so far – a doctor who had returned from DR Congo – in June.

The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way. The results should be available in three to six months, said Kaseya.

Of the total 10,091 cases, 10,060 have occurred in DR Congo, with 4,887 deaths. Two people have died in Uganda, and two in Kenya.

The response to the crisis has been hampered by inadequate protective equipment and unpaid health worker wages, leading to strikes. Conflict in DR Congo as well as mistrust towards officials in affected areas, misinformation and global aid cuts have further complicated the situation.

Kaseya will convene a meeting of African health ministers on Wednesday to urge greater cross-border cooperation. He wants governments to introduce screening and testing for people coming from affected regions at points of entry and exit.

“The main message to ministers is that they have to understand they could be affected, and we don’t want them to be surprised by what could happen,” he said.

At a meeting in November with African heads of state, Kaseya will call for a “corridor of peace” in conflict areas. “Currently, we have colleagues in Ituri who want to go and support the population, but they cannot because of insecurity,” he said. “I have to say to leaders, this outbreak is not for rebels, it’s not for the official army, it’s for everyone. Ebola can affect everyone … We need to come together to have a kind of agreement on how to protect each other.”

Kaseya called for a global effort to fund the response. He said governments had pledged $3bn (£2.3bn), but that more than $2bn was still outstanding. African countries had committed $120m, he said, while the rest is meant to come from international donors including the US, the UK and the EU.

“We need this money now,” he said. “We must understand that failure to provide funding now to African countries [will result in more being spent] because the outbreak will continue to move. If we have other countries affected we’ll be talking about trillions of dollars because it will require a lot of support to stop this outbreak.”

world.title: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’
world.snippet: Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected t...
world.content:
Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.

A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.

A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.

The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.

During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.

The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.

Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.

Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.

Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.

A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.

A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”

During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.

The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.
